links.reason: Kural 1302 warns that sulking kept too long spoils like too much salt; 316 names what is spoiled: those who could keep up sulking (புலந்து உறைதல் வல்லியோரே) end with fortune gone (செய்யோள் நீங்க), cooking a little food alone (சில்பதங் கொழித்து, தமியர்) while sons suck dried breasts. The friend's question வறிதுநீ புலத்தல் ஒல்லுமோ is the couplet's measure applied, and the economic turn is in the Tamil.

Both turn on புறப்புண் நாணி and வடக்கிருத்தல் at Venni. 65 mourns the stopping of a whole country (the five மறப்ப), and 66, to Karikal's face, after granting வென்றோய், asks நின்னினும் நல்லன் அன்றே; the pair shows the defeated king's death being ranked above the victory itself.

Venni is a real shared puram name, and the two akam poems do take opposite sides of it: 246 measures gossip by Azhundur's shout for Karikal (ஆர்ப்பினும் பெரிதே), 55 by Cheralathan's vadakkiruttal. But the image 55 uses is the noble men who chose to die with him (சான்றோர் ... அவனொடு செலீஇயர்), which the mother's life refuses to imitate, not a 'death beyond comfort'; the note and teaches blur that point.

Both dusk catalogues have the anril calling or settling in the palmyra's inner frond (பெண்ணை அகமடல் சேர / அகமடல் அகவ), with the sun sinking and lilies closing. In Kurinjippattu the catalogue ends at 230 and the next lines (231-232, நுமர்தர நாடறி நன்மணம் அயர்கம்) are the promise of marriage; 260's ends in midnight owls and ghosts (கழுதுவழங்கு அரைநாள்), so the shared formula takes its sense from its turn.

The epithet is genuinely shared (தீஞ்சுளைப் பலவின் நாஞ்சிற் பொருநன் / தடவுநிலைப் பலவின் நாஞ்சில் பொருநன்). But nothing in 380 refers to the elephant-for-rice story; that 140 'supplies the deed behind' 380 and that the fame 'rested on a story bards shared' is the proposer's construction, and the colophons even give different patrons (நாஞ்சில் வள்ளுவன், ஆய் அண்டிரன்), which the note does not mention.

231's புகழ் மாயலவே against the pyre that may shrink or reach the sky is an instance of 233's பொன்றாது நிற்பது ... புகழ். The pairing is mostly the shared topic (fame outlives death); the specific point 231 adds, that fame is independent of the pyre's size (குறுகுக / நீள்க), is not what teaches names.

Aay as a giver is a real shared name: 240 பாடுநர்க்கு அருகா ஆஅய் அண்டிரன், 152 வல்லினும் வல்லார் ஆயினும் சென்றோர்க்கு ... வீசும் ... ஆஅய். But 152 uses Aay's forest only to supply a feature of the woman, and nothing places it after his death, so 'outlived him as a landmark' while his poets scattered is an unsupported chronology. What 152 gives (வீசும் filling the deep pit) is not clearly elephants.

The exact phrase ஓர்எயில் மன்னன் against crowned kings occurs in both: 338's lone-fort lord refuses his daughter to the three garlanded வேந்தர், and 373's woman is sleepless like the lone-fort king whom kings have surrounded (வேந்தர் ஒருங்குஅகப் படுத்த). The akam poem takes only the sleepless watch; 'where the image came from' slightly overstates, but the shared puram situation is real.

109 makes Parambu's springs part of its unfailing plenty (மீன் கண் அற்று அதன் சுனையே); 176 cites the same springs (பாரி பறம்பிற் பனிச்சுனைத் தெண்ணீர்) as what those living by them scorned (ஓரூர் உண்மையின் இகழ்ந்தோர் போல), turning constancy into a lesson on neglecting a giver who is near. The extension is in the Tamil.

10 itself has the impartial inquiry (ஒப்ப நாடி அத்தக ஒறுத்தி), matching 541's ஓர்ந்து கண்ணோடாது ... தேர்ந்து செய்வது, and then adds the softening after submission (அடி பொருந்தி முந்தை நிற்பின் தண்டமும் தணிதி). So the pair shows mercy placed after the verdict, not favour inside it: a real qualification.

The gesture and verb are shared (இறைஞ்சினள் / இறைஞ்சினாள்), and 230 adds checked tears (பனிவரல் ஒடுக்கி). But the claim that the gesture is 'unreadable' to the man is the marker's reading: பெரிய எவ்வம் யாம் இவண் உற can simply be the pain of love her bowing causes, so 'the maxim is a reading made after the fact' needs a generous reading; 230 also lacks 1093's prior look (நோக்கினாள்).

Both argue on the hypothesis of no higher world: 222 மேலுலகம் இல்லெனினும் ஈதலே நன்று, 214 செய்யா உலகத்து நுகர்ச்சி இல்லெனின், மாறிப் பிறப்பின் இன்மையும் கூடும் ... தம்மிசை நட்டு. The Kural stops at 'it is good anyway', the king's chain of fallbacks still seeks a payoff (release, fame), which is a real and specific difference.

745 defines a good fort as hard to take, holding stored food (கொண்டகூழ்த்து) and easy to hold; 44's fort has no food or water (நெல்லுடைக் கவளமொடு ... பெறாஅ, பாலில் குழவி, நீரில் ... இனைகூஉ), so it simply fails 745's terms. 44 judges a king's conduct in a siege, 745 a fort's qualities: different situations, not incompatible claims.

The two address the same case: the glad giver. 159 says உவந்து நீ இன்புற விடுதி யாயின் சிறிது குன்றியும் கொள்வல், making gladness the condition that makes asking acceptable, while 1061 says even from those who give gladly without concealing (கரவாது உவந்தீயும்) not asking is worth a crore more. A genuine incompatibility on one point.

78 names Pari with Kapilar beside him (வாய்மொழிக் கபிலன் சூழ), holding out for years and driving off the kings (யாண்டுபல கழிய ... வேந்தர் ஓட்டிய), and uses Pari's pool (தீம்பெரும் பைஞ்சுனை) for the girl's fragrance; 109 is Kapilar's siege speech, with the same springs (மீன் கண் அற்று அதன் சுனையே). The note misses the shared spring, which strengthens the link, but what it says is accurate.

81 says household life exists to tend guests; 395 shows the chief handing the guest to his wife, பொன்போல் மடந்தையைக் காட்டி இவனை என்போல் போற்று, and the house keeps feeding him even in drought (33-38). The specific point, that the guest is placed in the household's care, not just fed once, is in the Tamil.

18 moves the meeting from night to day (பகல்நீ வரினும் புணர்குவை). In 12 the poem says only that the household holds her close and she will not live if he comes (நீ வரின் ... வாழலளே); the day meetings stopped and the demand for marriage are the colophon's (செறிப்பு, வரைவு கடாயது). The 'options closing one by one' is a sequence built across two poems from the thurai, and 18 does not build toward marriage.

218's maxim is about kind (சான்றோர் சான்றோர் பாலர் ஆப; சாலார் சாலார் பாலர்), not number, while 219 stresses that many sat with him (பலரால் அத்தை நின் குறிஇருந்தோரே). The claim that the laments treat the number of companions as the measure of worth misplaces 218's point, and 218 names no one; the tie rests on the colophon sequence.

Both are paalai poems where the man argues with a wealth-bent heart and paints desert killers. But 327's killers grieve only for the missed arrow (கொன்றோர் கோல்கழிபு இரங்கும்) and kill regardless of what is carried; only 337's Mazhavar kill a man thinking he might carry gold (பொன்னா குதலும் உண்டு). So 'the road weighing a life by what he might carry' holds for one poem only, and the pairing is mostly a shared paalai topic.

The shared line is striking (விண்பொரு நெடுங்குடை ... தேர் மோரியர் ... திகிரி திரிதர குறைத்த அறை), and the two uses differ as teaches says: in 69 a mark of how far he has gone. But in 175 the vehicle of the comparison is the sun's orb standing at the rock pass (அறைவாய் நிலைஇய மலர்வாய் மண்டிலத்து அன்ன), not 'the cutting's circle', so the note misdescribes the puram figure.

45 says the Chola civil war will only delight other kings (நும்மோர் அன்ன வேந்தர்க்கு மெய்ம்மலி உவகை செய்யும்); 58 says that if Chola and Pandya never break their union (உடனிலை திரியீர் ஆயின்) the earth will be theirs, and warns against outsiders (ஏதில் மாக்கள்) coming between them. The same calculation of who profits, from both sides.

1057 states the receiver's inner joy at a gift given without contempt (இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவாரைக் காணின்); 205 makes the manner a condition of acceptance even from the three kings (பெட்பின்றி ஈதல் யாம்வேண் டலமே). The move from feeling to condition is real and stated.

The rhetorical shape is genuinely shared: the comforting word is redirected to others (வாழ்வார்க்கு உரை / ஆற்றுவோர்க்கே). But teaches says 215's killers and vultures make visible 'the threat of death the Kural only implies'; in 1151 the implied death is the woman's left behind, while 215's road deaths are dangers to the traveller, so the claimed correspondence does not hold.

Both urge giving now because death is certain (நினக்கும் வருதல் வைகல் அற்றே / நாளைத் தழீஇம் ... படும்). The difference teaches names is real (359 offers lasting fame, இசையும் நிற்கும் ... நீடு விளங்கும்; Naladiyar 6 offers no reward), but it rests on one quatrain and the note's 'wealth is useless after the drum' is implied, not said. Mostly the shared topic.

A distinctive shared picture tied to Venkatam: 389 புன்தலை மடப்பிடி இனையக் கன்றுதந்து ... மன்றத்துப் பிணிக்கும் ... வேங்கடங் கிழவோன், 83 மடப்பிடி கானத்து அலறக் களிற்றுக் கன்று ஒழித்த ... பிணிக்கும் ... புல்லி ... வேங்கடம். In 83 Venkatam is a distance passed; in 389 it is the lord's epithet. 'Proof of wealth' slightly overstates 389, and the lords differ (Athanungan, Pulli), but the shared use is meaningful.

A tiger that prey cannot withstand is a common figure; 90 sets it on deer herds (மறப்புலி உடலின் மான்கணம் உளவோ), 599 on a huge, sharp-tusked elephant. Teaches' contrast of numbers and size is neat but thin; the image is not distinctive enough to make the pair more than a shared commonplace.

Two poems by different poets share only a paalai situation, the man speaking to his heart about wealth. 'The heart that raced home in 351 is restless again in 353' invents a sequence: 351's man is returning and pictures her waiting, 353's is home and argues from passing days and age (நாளது செலவும் மூப்பினது வரவும்) and her hospitality; neither refers to the other.

34 quotes the rule as dharma's saying (செய்தி கொன்றோர்க்கு உய்தி இல், with the lesser crimes that have expiation, கழுவாயும் உள), and 110 states it as a maxim (செய்ந்நன்றி கொன்ற மகற்கு உய்வில்லை). 34 applies it to the poet himself (பாடேன் ஆயின் படுபறி யலனே பல்கதிர்ச் செல்வன்), which is what teaches says.

The tension is real: 1066 says asking even water for a cow degrades the tongue (இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்), while 327 praises the நெடுந்தகை who asks millet face to face (முகத்தவை கூறி வரகுடன் இரக்கும்) to relieve his kin's want (ஒக்கல் ஒற்கம் சொலிய). But teaches overstates in claiming the pair 'shows' the shame of asking was a later rule; two verses cannot date an ethic.

216 puts the fruit tree in the heart of town (உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்றால்), reachable by all; 119 puts the giver as a lone tree on a long shadeless road (நிழலில் நீளிடைத் தனிமரம் போல), giving beyond drum-rich kings (பணைகெழு வேந்தரை இறந்தும்). Placement turns the figure from accessibility to scarcity. The poem itself does not name Pari; that is from the poet and context.

12's இன்னா ஆகப் பிறர் மண் கொண்டு does meet 659's அழக் கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம. But 12 is a question that can be read as playful praise, and the Kural cannot show that the poet's irony 'carries a real moral charge'; the link holds only on one reading of 12, and calling it AGREES assumes that reading.

The phrase is shared (புதுவது அன்று / சாதலும் புதுவது அன்றே). 192 uses the oldness of death for calm toward great and small (பெரியோரை வியத்தலும் இலமே), while 76 concedes it only to set off what is new (இன்றின் ஊங்கோ கேளலம்): one king against seven. Opposite uses of one commonplace, accurately stated.

Both are மூதின் முல்லை and the contrast is real, but the note misassigns 312's duties: the father's share is சான்றோன் ஆக்குதல், and sending the son out is assigned to no one; the spear is the smith's (வேல்வடித்துக் கொடுத்தல் கொல்லற்குக் கடனே). In 279 the mother gives the spear herself (வேல்கைக் கொடுத்து), a sharper point the teaches misses while claiming she takes over the father's task.

Both refuse comfort that rests on a promise of a quick return: 229 sets his own words, இன்னே வருதும் எனத் தெளித்தோரே, against the spring's cuckoo (இன்இள வேனிலும் வாரார்), and 1151 sends the promise of வல்வரவு to those who will be alive then. Teaches correctly marks the difference in moment: before parting in the Kural, proof after the fact in the poem.

The two friends' comforts do rest on different grounds: in 173 his maxim and the gesture (அறம் தலைப்பிரியாது ... எல்வளை திருத்தினர் ஆயின் வருவர்), in 177 his memory of her body (தொய்யிலை நினைந்தே ... வல்லே வருவர்). But neither poem limits the other, so QUALIFIES does not fit, and the lesson is modest: two variants of the வற்புறுத்தல் situation.

Pittan's spear against hostile kings is in both: 172 ஆரமர் கடக்கும் வேலும் ... மாறுகொள் மன்னரும், 77 பொருந்தா மன்னர் அருஞ்சமத்து உயர்த்த திருந்துஇலை எஃகம். Both also tie him to the Chera overlord (கோதை / வானவன் மறவன்) and to toddy (கள்ளும் குறைபடல் ஓம்புக / ஆனா நறவின்). The akam poet makes the patron's weapon the measure of her eyes' wound, as teaches says.

The two poems share a striking image: rags like pond moss stripped off and new cloth put on (முதுநீர்ப் பாசி அன்ன உடைகளைந்து ... புதுமடிக் கொளீஇ / பாசி வேர்புரை சிதாஅர் நீக்கி ... கலிங்கம் உடீஇ). But changing a bard's rags for cloth is the general parisil scene, not shown to be an Athiyar 'house custom', and 390 also ends in plunder (கொண்டி பெறுக), so conquest is not what 392 adds. 390's patron is only from the colophon.

335 urges hurrying to good deeds before the death rattle; 195, to old men who have done none, sets a floor: நல்லது செய்தல் ஆற்றீர் ஆயினும் அல்லது செய்தல் ஓம்புமின், and says this too is நல்லாற்றுப் படூஉம் நெறி. A genuine limit added to the Kural's demand, stated in the Tamil.

110 is Kapilar's siege boast to the three kings (மூவிரும் கூடி ... பறம்பு கொள்ற்கு அரிதே; யாமும் பாரியும் உளமே), and 78 recalls Pari with Kapilar at his side driving off the kings over years (கபிலன் சூழ ... யாண்டுபல கழிய ... வேந்தர் ஓட்டிய), as a simile for the girl. The pairing of Kapilar with Pari in both makes the puram-to-akam reuse concrete.

Both are the woman telling her friend the promised rains have come without him (காலை வந்தன்றால் காரே / கார்மன் இதுவால்), and the colophons file them as paalai and mullai, which is a real observation about classification. But it is one situation in one domain, so PARALLEL_DOMAIN is wrong, and what the pair teaches is about the colophons, not the poems.

Both turn on a broken assurance: 1154 asks whether those who trusted (தெளித்தசொல் தேறியார்க்கு) are at fault, putting it as blame; akananuru 1 asks whether he has forgotten his word (பிரியலம் என்ற சொல்தாம் மறந்தனர் கொல்லோ), keeping it a question of memory. The two treat the same situation differently, as teaches says.
links.text_issue: akananuru:1 line 5 recurs in akananuru:356 line 9.

links.reason: Chezhiyan (செழியன்) is a dynastic name borne by several Pandyas; 116's battle is at Koodal against two kings (இருபெரு வேந்தர்), 76's against seven at Thalaiyalanganam, and the note admits they may differ. Teaches still speaks of 'his fame' as one king's, which needs an identity the Tamil does not give.

The link needs two unproven steps: that Vattaru's Ezhiniyathan (396) and Chelli's Athan Ezhini (216) are one man, on the strength of the Kosar appearing in both, and one reading of 216 lines 12-15, where it is unclear whether the Chelli lord's spear struck Ezhini or Ezhini's spear struck the elephant (the note and the marked reading of 216 disagree). 'The patron's two reputations' is built on both guesses.

1141's அலர் is the public talk about the lovers, which keeps a lover's life going (அலரெழ ஆருயிர் நிற்கும்); 183's புறங்கூறல் is backbiting, and the life in question is the backbiter's own (புறங்கூறிப் பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல்). The note calls the அலர் backbiting, which misreads 1141, and the two verses make no claims about the same thing.

poems.note: The tiger killing the elephant is only heard as a sound of the waste; it does nothing a lover does.
The lone herdsman guarding his flock at night could hint at her guarded chastity (முல்லை சான்ற கற்பின்), but only one correspondence can be anchored.

iraicchi.act: the wildcat's kitten keeps close behind its mother, like stars around the moon (மதிசூழ் மீனின் தாய்வழிப் படூஉம்)
iraicchi.sense: she who said she would come with him (வருவல் என்றோள்) would cling to him like the kitten, which makes leaving her through this forest harder

iraicchi.act: the male monkey reaches for jackfruit to ease his mate's hunger, yet even touching it on the guarded slope brings danger
iraicchi.sense: the hero's approach to the closely guarded girl is perilous, so he should provide for her properly by marriage

poems.note: Lines 12-14 are hard to construe; the guard comparison (மகளிர் மாங்காட்டு அற்றே) is open, the monkey pair is not.

iraicchi.act: the male wildcat waits for the rooster's unguarded moment to end his hungry mate's hunger (ஊன்நசைப் பிணவின் உயங்குபசி களைஇயர்)
iraicchi.sense: even the wildcat stays and provides for his mate at dusk, while her man is away and the evening is sweet only for those together

iraicchi.act: the small sea crow rests at midnight on the thazhai branch with its lovely mate, dreaming of prawns
iraicchi.sense: even the crow keeps its mate by it through the night, while the lord leaves her alone in her sorrow

poems.note: The female kite's long calls might be read as calling a mate, but the poem names no mate and no act toward one.

The opening tusker, wounded by a tiger, its wound unwashed in the night's rain, maps the man's night visits (tusker = man, tiger fight = the night path's dangers); the later elephant (ஒருத்தலின் பெயர்குவை) is an open simile and kept apart.
Puram poem (பெருந்திணை in Purananuru): null by rule.
